subtype_info: intestinal tuberculosis presenting as small bowel obstruction
title: Revisiting the Era of Intestinal Tuberculosis: A Case Presenting As Small Bowel Obstruction With Classical Imaging and Histopathological Appearances
case_text:
A 49-year-old man was admitted to a tertiary care hospital serving a rural population in central India. He complained of abdominal pain and abdominal distension for one and a half months. He also complained of constipation for the last couple of months. On examination, the abdomen was rigid, distended, and tender. Guarding of the abdomen was present. An erect abdominal radiograph revealed dilated loops of the small intestine with multiple air-fluid levels suggestive of small intestine obstruction (Figure 1).
A contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen was performed. It showed multiple strictures involving the distal jejunum and ileum, causing small intestine obstruction. Mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy with central necrosis was observed along with mild to moderate ascites (Figures 2, 3).
The radiological findings favored an infectious or inflammatory etiology with a more likely possibility of intestinal TB than Crohn's disease. Clinical and histopathological correlation was recommended. The patient underwent surgery for acute small bowel obstruction. Intraoperative findings of multiple strictures in the ileum and jejunum were observed, as well as many enlarged lymph nodes. We received a 62 cm long specimen of the resected bowel, which contained the jejunum, ileum, and caecum with a small part of the ascending colon. A total of four strictures were identified. The serosal surface had many tiny nodules/tubercles (Figure 4). A total of 22 lymph nodes were identified.
Microscopy revealed mucosal ulceration at the site of the stricture. Multiple caseating granulomas were identified spread across the mucosa, submucosa extending to serosa along with extensive fibrosis. The Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) staining highlighted acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Fourteen out of the 22 lymph nodes showed granulomatous reaction and ZN staining did not reveal any AFB (Figure 5).
A diagnosis of intestinal tuberculosis (ITB) was made. The patient has started a six-month regimen of isoniazid (H), rifampicin (R), ethambutol (E), and pyrazinamide (Z), all four drugs for the first two months, followed by H and R for the remaining four months.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: intestinal tuberculosis presenting as small bowel obstruction
